summary: POC scoping focused on capacity hedging: reserved GPUs for baseline throughput, configurable burst lanes for traffic spikes, and automated fallback chains (model variants -> queued routing -> degraded mode). Discussed benchmark plan, success criteria (latency, cost, fidelity), timeline for a 4-week pilot, and remaining security questions.
meeting_header: Date: 2028-06-12 | Start: 16:00 PDT | Duration: 58m | Location: Zoom | Recording: yes | Attendees: Alex Mercer (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Solaris Infra Lead), Carlos Mendez (Solaris CTO), Marta Ruiz (Solaris PM)
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Mercer: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We'll run through the POC scope — capacity, benchmarks, and the fallback playbook. Samir and I will mostly cover technical sizing. Priya, Carlos, Marta, thanks for your time.
[00:18] Priya Nair: Yeah thanks. Quick context from our side — we are moving from an internal microservice that calls a third party LLM API to bringing inference in-house for cost and latency. Need predictable tail latency for customer-facing features.
[00:34] Samir Patel: Great, that's helpful. Can you confirm expected steady-state QPS and what spike patterns look like? e.g. hourly spikes vs bursty fanouts?
[00:47] Marta Ruiz: Our typical is 120 reqs/min average between 08:00-20:00 and then we have periodic product launches where we see a 10x spike for 10-30 minutes. Also a couple of internal batch jobs overnight.
[01:03] Carlos Mendez: Important: p95 must stay below 350 ms for interactive UI and p99 below 900 ms. These are our customer SLAs.
[01:13] Alex Mercer: Ok that gives us constraints. For the POC we usually recommend sizing reserved GPUs to cover baseline throughput plus a safety buffer — sounds like baseline is around 2 rps average (120/min) with 10x spikes.
[01:28] Priya Nair: Sorry, did you mean 2 rps per model instance? We have multi-tenant traffic and some requests are multi-turn, so token counts vary.
[01:37] Samir Patel: Right, need workload shape. For the POC send us 7 days of traces including sample payload sizes. For now assume 800 tokens average per request for the interactive flow. If that's high we can adjust.
[01:49] Marta Ruiz: We'll extract traces today.
[01:52] Alex Mercer: For math simplicity — if average request costs 800 tokens, then token/sec and GPU throughput will drive reserved sizing. For this POC we propose a reserved pool sized to meet baseline p95 SLAs with continuous batching. Then configure burst lanes that pull from a burst pool with preemptible GPUs for spikes.
[02:09] [02:10] Priya Nair: How does preemption affect in-flight requests? We can't drop user requests mid-conversation.
[02:18] Samir Patel: Good point. Preemptible burst nodes are for short-lived extra capacity; we do graceful draining — new requests queue for a few seconds while KV cache is preserved. If nodes are reclaimed we automatically route to lower-cost model variants (quantized or smaller family) or to hosted fallback per policy.
[02:35] Carlos Mendez: We want to avoid quality regressions. If routed to a smaller model, how do we surface that?
[02:42] Alex Mercer: Redwood has a routing header and telemetry flag that tags responses with model variant and quality score. We can surface that to your product for metric-based gating. Also the rollout policy can prefer latency over fidelity only when error budget triggers.
[02:55] [03:00] Marta Ruiz: Can we set a business rule: if model variant changes, degrade to read-only mode or maybe show a subtle latency spinner?
[03:09] Samir Patel: Yes you can. We'll capture that as an acceptance test: detect any response that uses variant != primary and ensure UI shows fallback.
[03:17] Priya Nair: Back to sizing, what about KV/cache warmup — warm caches drastically reduce token cost for multi-turn. How does Redwood handle cold starts for new sessions?
[03:29] Samir Patel: We do prefix caching at the route level — for POC we recommend maintaining a small pool of warmed workers pinned to sticky sessions if you have heavy multi-turn. That is a config option on Dedicated or Private. For hosted POC we can simulate sticky affinity during benchmark runs.
[03:46] [03:50] Alex Mercer: Let's outline the benchmark plan now: 1) baseline steady-state test for 2 hours at average QPS; 2) step spike test to 10x for 30 minutes; 3) sudden fanout test with 500 concurrent new sessions; 4) long tail tests for p95/p99 measurement. Samir will provide the harness.
[04:06] Samir Patel: I will provide a k6 harness and a small runner that emits the same header structure so we can reproduce prefix caching. We'll also include a prom + jaeger export example.
[04:15] Carlos Mendez: How do we interpret cost during the test? We need per-token cost and per-minute GPU cost so finance can evaluate.
[04:23] Alex Mercer: We'll give a detailed POC estimate: reserved pool cost (fixed) + burst pool cost (metered) + data egress and observability add-ons. For the POC period we can cap burst spend and set alerts.
[04:34] Priya Nair: Security check — KMS integration, SSO, and audit logs. We need to know what the private deployment timeline is if we go that route.
[04:43] Samir Patel: Private deploy is an extra effort. For the POC we'll do it on Redwood Dedicated in your cloud VPC with customer-managed KMS for encryption-at-rest; SAML SSO and audit logs are available. Private on-prem would take longer. We'll share a security doc.
[04:57] [05:00] Marta Ruiz: What about network egress — we have strict data residency rules for EU users.
[05:05] Alex Mercer: We support region pinning for routes. For the POC, run in your preferred region. We'll include data residency in the security package.
[05:13] Carlos Mendez: Ok timeline — you said four weeks earlier?
[05:17] Alex Mercer: Typical POC flow: week 0 onboarding and credentialing + harness setup; week 1 baseline runs and sizing adjustments; week 2 spike and resilience tests; week 3 run extended soak and finalize success criteria. We can compress to 3 weeks if Solaris is ready and provides traces quickly.
[05:33] Priya Nair: Who owns the benchmark runs? Our infra team or Redwood?
[05:36] Samir Patel: We can run them jointly. We'll give the harness and a checklist; ideally you run in your environment for realistic network characteristics. We'll also run controlled replicate jobs to compare.
[05:47] [06:00] Alex Mercer: Let's capture acceptance criteria now: - p95 < 350 ms for baseline flow for 95% of test time - p99 < 900 ms during steady-state - During spike, maintain p95 < 700 ms (or failover to designated degraded mode) - Fidelity: <3% metric delta on the business score compared to baseline model - Cost: reserved capacity utilization >50% to justify reserved pool - No data sent to third parties, KMS at rest, SSO enabled.
[06:28] Marta Ruiz: That <3% fidelity delta — we need to define the business score, we'll provide the exact metric.
[06:33] Alex Mercer: Perfect. We'll parameterize the acceptance tests.
[06:36] [06:45] Priya Nair: A practical question — how quickly can Redwood spin up burst nodes? In our experience with cloud autoscaling it can take a minute or two, that's critical for UX.
[06:52] Samir Patel: Typical cold provision for GPUs is ~60-120s depending on instance type. To mitigate that we use multiple levers: 1) a small warm standby fleet of pre-warmed instances on hot routes, 2) continuous micro-batching to reduce need for more nodes, and 3) preemptible fast-lane nodes with faster start times if you opt into them.
[07:12] Alex Mercer: We can set the policy to begin queuing for up to 10s before spinning up burst nodes if the queue trend shows sustained growth; that buys you a few seconds of smoothing.
[07:22] [07:30] Carlos Mendez: If the burst capacity isn't available and we route to a smaller model, what metrics do we log so we can reconcile customer impact?
[07:38] Samir Patel: All responses include metadata: model name, quantization level, latency, tokens consumed, and a quality score we compute based on your eval rubric. We'll also produce a daily reconciliation sheet for the POC.
[07:50] Marta Ruiz: Can you show an example of the fallback chain? I want to see precise order and policies.
[07:55] Alex Mercer: Example fallback chain: 1) primary reserved pool (primary model) 2) burst pool (same model, preemptible) 3) smaller variant (e.g., 7B quantized) 4) queue with graceful degradation mode (UI shows limited responses) 5) last resort route to hosted high-latency failover with disclaimer. Each step has thresholds (CPU/GPU util, queue depth, time).
[08:17] [08:20] Priya Nair: For step 3, do we apply a confidence gating or just route automatically?
[08:26] Samir Patel: You can configure a hybrid: route automatically but tag responses and trigger an offline quality monitor. Or only route if queue depth exceeds X and latency > Y. We'll recommend gating in the POC.
[08:36] Alex Mercer: Also note that some of our customers prefer a canary rule: route 5% of traffic to variant to monitor real-world quality before influencing 100% automatic fallback. That's an option.
[08:46] [09:00] Carlos Mendez: Budget guardrails — we need hard caps. Can you cap burst spend and set automated drain?
[09:06] Alex Mercer: Yes, POC configs can include a burst spend cap that disables automatic burst beyond threshold and sends us an alert. We'll also set a safety policy to favor latency degradation over cost by default only if you choose.
[09:17] Priya Nair: Regarding observability, we need token-level costs and per-route breakdowns.
[09:23] Samir Patel: Console exposes token-level cost and per-route latency histograms. For the POC we give extended retention for the test window and a shared dashboard. We'll export CSVs for finance.
[09:33] Marta Ruiz: Security again — audit logs: do they show token contents or just metadata? We can't store PII.
[09:39] Alex Mercer: Audit logs store metadata only: timestamps, route, model, token counts; payload content is redacted by default. If you need payload-level logging for debugging, it requires an explicit opt-in and retention policy.
[09:54] [10:00] Priya Nair: One more operational question: how are KV caches persisted across restarts? If we preempt a node, will we lose context and force re-gen?
[10:09] Samir Patel: We persist KV cache to a fast in-memory store that is replicated across warm workers. If a worker is reclaimed the cache is recovered within seconds for sticky sessions, but absolute cold-starts will require re-generation. That's why for heavy multi-turn the sticky pool is recommended.
[10:24] Alex Mercer: Let's record a few risk items: 1) cache cold-starts during high churn; 2) burst node preemption under high cloud demand; 3) fidelity drift when routing to smaller models. We'll include mitigation steps.
[10:37] [10:45] Carlos Mendez: Can you put together an SLO/SLI doc for our legal team? They'll want formal language.
[10:51] Alex Mercer: Yep Samir will draft an SLO doc, and we'll include default remediation and credits for the POC if SLOs aren't met — subject to scope.
[10:59] Priya Nair: Good. On the timeline I'll aim to share request traces by Friday.
[11:04] Marta Ruiz: And I'll produce the business success metrics.
[11:07] Alex Mercer: Great. Any other blocking questions?
[11:10] [11:20] Priya Nair: One tiny point: latency budget for mobile clients is stricter, maybe p95 250ms. Can we target a mobile route with stricter controls?
[11:27] Samir Patel: Yes we can create a dedicated mobile route with higher prioritization and a smaller fanout. That would require reserving some capacity exclusively for mobile. We'll include that as an optional line item in pricing.
[11:38] Alex Mercer: Alright let's recap next steps — we'll share pricing, security docs, benchmark harness and runbook. Solaris will share traces and success criteria. We'll tentatively schedule the onboarding session for week of 06/19.
[11:54] Carlos Mendez: Sounds good. Thank you.
[11:58] Alex Mercer: Thanks team. We'll follow up by email.
[12:00] -- End of recording --
